questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The subjects offered by the university and the career path I have chosen as of now match.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Culturally very different academic wise which was interesting but also hard to adjust to. All of the exams were closed book exams, which meant no notes or any means of help. It is very much focused on memory and not so much logically applying law as in KU. It made sense for the subjects like Contemporary history, not so much for international private/public law.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: 5/10, it was quite a journey to find the correct information and all of us were very confused. Their introduction was a waste of time, as it was only meant for the Spanish students and did not once mention anything about exchange students. Also it was in spanish so only like 2 of the exchange students understood anything (which was irrelevant anyways as it was all directed towards the spanish students).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The assistant teacher joined our whatsapp group and helped with most information which was very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Difficult but it depends on your preference. It is near impossible finding an apartment by yourself if the lease is below 6 months, so i would highly suggest finding roommates to share with (also for the experience). There are a few scammers out there as well so beware and do not pay anything online (directly to a person) unless it is a verified website such as Spotahome.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I did not even know there was a campus. I don't know anyone who lived on campus but it is pretty much like in Denmark. I enjoyed having a place ~15-20 minutes in metro out of the city near the university. Considering attendence is mandatory and you can expect to go to school pretty much every single day, I felt it was a good idea to live near the school instead of the city. 5 days school vs. the weekend for partying.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was difficult but doable. I did choose the hard way though, but there are many facebook groups such as Erasmus in Madrid where you can find roommates to share housing with.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Oh my, it is a gruelling process. You first have to navigate through their website which by the way is a maze. Once you reach the folder offering academic courses, half of them are not available. 25% of them are in Spanish only and considering you have to make your own schedule with 5 subjects of 6 ECTS each, it is near impossible to figure out as you also have to beware of overlapping classes. I ended up after over 20 hours of struggling with matching a schedule. It was one where I had to go to class at 8-10 am and then again at 1-3 pm every day. They have placed every class taught in english between 1 and 7 pm which makes it even tougher.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We were able to enter Excellencia classes because of the impossibility of making a schedule otherwise.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I did not get every class I wished for but in the end, I was successful registering for 5 classes with no overlaps.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared to spend a lot of time creating a schedule with classes you may have regrets about. Fortunately it is possible for the first 2 weeks to try out different classes to see which ones you enjoy. The unfortunate part is that you miss 2 weeks of classes in the end for the ones you choose as you won't have time for all of them and miss the introductions/first lectures.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It would be nice with more courses in English for exchange students and spreading out the timing of classes a bit more.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The requirements to pass are definitely lower standard than UCPH. It does not take that much effort to pass the course as long as you follow the classes. The classes are the syllabus, you do not get any books and the professors make the exams.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I liked some of the classes' way of teaching, especially international public law and keys to contemporary history. It takes some time getting used to the teachers' Spanglish decyphering what they say at times. It felt a lot like highschool with mandatory attendance and the way of grading was different. The grade is divided from 100% into sections where a group project counts for 10%, activity in class for 10%, partial exams for 20%, essays/assignments for 10% and the final exam for 50%. I did enjoy the fact that the grade is a pass/fail and does not account for whether you get 100% or 50%, as long as you are above 50%, you pass.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Keys to contemporary history, Roman law, Private international law, Public international law, UN and other international organizations.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Keys to contemporary history was easy, as it is litterally just history dating from the declaration of independence in the US to the Cold war. Public international law was great because of Allan's teaching style, which i truly enjoyed a lot. If a subject is taught by Allan Tatham, you can rest assured that it'll be fun.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed using Freenow (Taxi service) quite a bit as it is pretty cheap. It is important to remember to get a personal travelcard which you pay 20 euro for per month to use the metro/bus/etc. This can be done through CityLife online or in a person in Madrid.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Pretty much everything is cheaper than in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not bother, I made friends by through class or from facebook/whatsapp groups, such as Madrid Urban Vibes/Meet new People Madrid, etc. They host events such as pubcrawls etc.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: No idea.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely going out and being a part of the culture and make friends. Try using one of the whatsapp/facebook groups for activities. Or you could try something completely different, personally I started learning Bachata Sensual which was a great experience and I enjoyed it a lot and met many people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely explore other cities such as Barcelona for the tourist attractions and the gothic architecture. I would recommend the walking tours. You could visit Málaga for the beach vibe. Valencia was great as it is the origin city of Paella, so that is a must (also try Horchata in the Santa Catalina Horchataria).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It is a pretty relaxed culture where nobody is in a hurry. It is normal to be late which is quite difficult to adjust to as a Dane.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Definitely make an effort and ask if they are down to do anything or go out. Most of the spanish students just interact with eachother and it can be tough if you are not an extrovert.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The Spaniards being late to everything. I just cannot.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The people were super friendly and it is a very collectivistic culture in contrast to the danish individualistic one. An example is that people strike up a conversation in public transport and sit next to you with no problem, which is a big nono in Denmark. At the gym, a random guy asked if I wanted to join him in his workout and that is now a great friend of mine.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
LEARN SPANISH - even if it is just a few basic words and continue with it. I regret not getting making a greater effort. Nobody speaks English so keep your google translate open because you will need it.
Explore not just Madrid but also the adjacent cities. I used the speedtrain (Renfe) a lot, as it only took 2 hours to Valencia/Barcelona and i preferred paying a bit more to avoid an 8 hour busride with Alsa. 
My motto was "why not" to practically anything. New experiences in particular whether it was food, going out to a club, trying a dickwaffle in Chueca (the gay neighbourhood). I met a girl in a club during a pubcrawl and we instantly become friends and the next day we went to Valencia together because why not? And she is now one of my closest friends. 
Academic wise I would say - stay above 75% attendance and definitely make sure you do your work as it will make the final exam count less towards your final grade. Classes are your books and everything the professor says can be on your exam, so take notes because not all courses are recorded. Also definitely ask someone for notes if you miss a class.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid of trying new things.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made, my spanish improved very much and I don't need google translate anymore. The experience of travelling abroad which also helps the CV.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Definitely an experience you would not regret. It is an emotional rollercoaster with ups and downs and was nervewrecking. Being alone in a country, knowing nobody, and not speaking the language can be difficult. But once you get over the initial stage and start exploring and making friends, it becomes easy and fun. 
The courses were a pain to get going as well so that was probably the greatest challenge.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
